capability.h1: How much useful work can AI complete reliably?
capability.summary: Newer AI models handle longer technical tasks in benchmarks. Reliable performance across whole jobs remains uncertain.
capability.selection: Feature METR to track technical-task progress at an explicit success rate, with published uncertainty. Use RLI as related evidence on finished projects beyond software.
capability.gap: Repeated, independent tests of reliable performance across whole workflows, including work beyond software.

sources.title: Remote Labor Index: projects meeting the reference standard
sources.locate: Performance Comparison, first row and legend; Core Metrics; original paper sections 3.2-3.4.
sources.label: Professional project completion
sources.date: Leaderboard read 13 October 2026; row evaluation date unclear
sources.finding: The leading listed agent scores 21.25% on the Remote Labor Index, which compares AI outputs with reference deliverables from freelance projects.
sources.why: An interpretable completion measure on professional work, with inspectable project examples.
sources.limit: Selected benchmark projects, not actual jobs or client acceptance. Scale AI is a commercial research partner. Do not infer a dated trend from model release dates.
metrics: Not a share of jobs replaced
checks: Confirm 21.25% is the automation score, not Elo, and record the retrieval date.
Check grading, project denominator and evaluation setup before approving a historical curve.

sources.title: METR task-completion horizons at 80% success
sources.locate: Definition, Methodological Details and Updates; linked TH1.1 YAML, all records released from 2023 onward, metrics.p80_horizon_length and release_date.
sources.label: Reliability on longer tasks
sources.finding: At 80% success, the estimated task horizon rises from under one minute for GPT-4 (March 2023) to about three hours for Claude Mythos Preview (early, April 2026). The chart includes all 23 tested models released from 2023 onward, not just these endpoints.
sources.why: Makes reliability explicit in human-equivalent task time, with downloadable results and uncertainty estimates.
sources.limit: Technical tasks, not whole jobs or agent runtime. The latest point has a wide 95% interval of 1.6-6.6 hours. Release dates are not evaluation dates. The tracker is no longer actively updated.
checks: Check the definition and stopped-update notice: task difficulty is not unattended runtime.
In the linked YAML, check all release dates, p80_horizon_length estimates and 95% intervals against the downloadable chart data.

adoption.h1: How common is regular AI use at work?
adoption.summary: Regular AI use among US employees rose from 11% in May 2023 to 32% in August 2026. Use is spreading; how much work is delegated remains unclear.
adoption.selection: Feature Gallup's repeated measure of frequent AI use by US employees. Use Eurostat for separate context on EU businesses, without combining populations or definitions.
adoption.gap: Track the share of work actually delegated, how outputs are checked, and whether people can still do the work without AI.

sources.title: Gallup regular workplace AI use
sources.locate: Use of AI table, Frequent AI users column, eight rows from 5/1/23 to 8/1/26; Survey Methods above the table.
sources.label: Regular workplace AI use
sources.finding: The share of US employees using AI at work a few times a week or more rose from 11% in May 2023 to 32% in August 2026, a 21-percentage-point increase.
sources.why: Repeated, probability-based employee surveys across occupations. The frequent-use category distinguishes regular use from occasional experimentation.
sources.limit: US employees aged 18+ working for organisations. Self-reported AI use, not work automated or dependence. The table is newer than parts of the surrounding prose; wave-specific intervals are not supplied there.
metrics: A few times a week or more, May 2023
A few times a week or more, August 2026
checks: Check all eight Frequent AI users values and dates; daily users are included, not added separately.
Confirm US employee eligibility; do not call this a share of all adults, work hours or automated tasks.

sources.title: Eurostat enterprise AI use
sources.locate: Opening paragraph and Methodological notes in the dated news release; Data sources and Netherlands break note in Statistics Explained.
sources.label: AI use by EU businesses
sources.finding: 20.0% of covered EU enterprises used AI in 2025, up from 13.5% in 2024.
sources.why: Adds official, recurring measurement outside the US with a defined business population.
sources.limit: Businesses with 10 or more people in covered sectors; excludes microfirms. Broad AI, not just generative AI. A new AI category in 2025 and a Netherlands series break complicate year-to-year comparisons.
checks: Verify both annual values and the 10-person cutoff in the release.
Check sectors, AI definition and the Netherlands break before interpreting the change.

handover.h1: How much work do people hand over to AI?
handover.summary: In May 2026, 48.6% of classified Claude chat and Cowork conversations were labelled automation. Whether people checked or used the output is not observed.
handover.selection: Feature Anthropic's observed interaction patterns, which distinguish task completion from collaboration. Keep the UK regulator survey as narrower, provisional context on decision autonomy.
handover.gap: An independent measure across providers of which decisions AI makes, which people review, and which people can reverse.

sources.title: Anthropic Economic Index: automation and augmentation
sources.locate: June release CSV: May 2026, GLOBAL, overall, collaboration_bucket_automation_pct and collaboration_bucket_augmentation_pct. Data documentation defines metrics and platform coverage.
sources.label: Automation versus augmentation
sources.date: Claude chat and Cowork, May 2026; June release
sources.finding: Among conversations assigned either mode, 48.62% were classified as automation and 51.38% as augmentation. The 2.61% labelled 'None' is outside this denominator, as verified from component totals.
sources.why: Observed interaction patterns are closer to delegation than counts of users. The underlying data are downloadable.
sources.limit: One provider's classifier. Automation is not autonomy or absence of oversight. May 2026 includes chat and Cowork; sampling changes prevent a simple comparison with older releases.
metrics: Automation among conversations assigned either mode
checks: Check the May GLOBAL overall CSV rows and normalized bucket denominator; unclassified conversations are excluded.
Review the provider classification and distinguish automation from decision autonomy or human review.

sources.title: Bank of England/FCA: autonomy of AI use cases
sources.locate: Section 1.2 Methodology; executive-summary Automated decision-making bullets; section 2.5 and Chart 7.
sources.label: Autonomy in financial services
sources.finding: The survey distinguishes partial automation from full autonomy. Its firms-versus-use-cases denominator needs reconciliation before percentages are featured.
sources.why: Directly distinguishes partial automation from full autonomy, in a survey independent of AI providers.
sources.limit: Firm self-report in one sector, not decision volumes. The chart subtitle and narrative use different denominator wording; retain a provisional label until reconciled.
checks: Read section 2.5 and methodology; confirm the 118 respondents and definitions.
Resolve Chart 7's firms/use-cases wording before citing. Do not add the overlapping percentages.

work.h1: Are entry-level jobs becoming harder to find?
work.summary: In the ADP sample, employment among ages 22–25 fell 12.8% in the most AI-exposed occupations from November 2022 to August 2026. The least-exposed group rose 8.1%; AI causation is not established.
work.selection: Feature Stanford/ADP's monthly age-by-exposure payroll series, with all five quintiles visible. Keep Danish adoption-linked counterevidence separate because its population, outcome and period differ.
work.gap: Link firms' AI adoption to junior hiring and training, with comparisons that separate AI from other changes in the labour market.

sources.title: Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence
sources.locate: Employment Index by Age Group and AI Exposure; September 2026 data package, Early Career 1 (22-25), all five quintiles, November 2022 = 100.
sources.label: Young workers in exposed occupations
sources.date: September 2026 dashboard release; data through August 2026
sources.finding: From November 2022 to August 2026, the most-exposed quintile's employment index fell from 100 to 87.23; the least-exposed rose to 108.1, among ages 22-25 in the ADP sample.
sources.why: A repeatable age-by-exposure comparison, with detailed discussion of alternative explanations.
sources.limit: Descriptive, not jobs proven lost to AI. Exposure is not adoption; sample selection, education and pre-trends affect interpretation.
checks: Check the September package, ages 22-25, quintile definitions, baseline and all 60 monthly values.
Do not apply the earlier pooled 19% June shortfall to this chart's extreme-quintile August endpoints.

sources.title: Still Waters, Rapid Currents: Early Labor Market Transformation under Generative AI
sources.locate: March 13, 2026 author PDF: sections 1.1-1.3; section 3.4, PDF page 31; Figure 8 caption, PDF page 47.
sources.label: Adoption-linked counterevidence
sources.finding: Workplaces encouraging chatbot use showed no extra decline in their share of workers aged 22-25 through 2024.
sources.why: Links adoption information to administrative outcomes, rather than treating occupational exposure as actual use.
sources.limit: Encouragement was not randomized. Different country and period from the US study; this does not rule out later displacement.
metrics: Not a test of later US effects
checks: Read section 3.4 / Figure 8: ages, employment-share outcome, comparison and endpoint.
Check the linked survey/register design; do not call encouragement randomized.

share.h1: How much economic output goes to workers?
share.summary: The ILO estimates labour's global GDP share fell from 53.0% in 2015 to 52.6% in 2025. This modest decline predates widespread generative AI and does not identify its effect.
share.selection: Feature ILO global labour income share for international coverage, including self-employment. Keep the more frequent BLS US sector measure as separate context, not another point on the same chart.
share.gap: Measure changes in labour income alongside actual AI adoption, at firm and sector level, with comparable definitions over time.

sources.title: Labor share at its lowest level, 52.8 percent, in second quarter 2026
sources.locate: BLS Economics Daily, September 15, 2026: opening paragraph and Chart Data table; FRED PRS85006173 unit label.
sources.label: US labour share
sources.finding: Labour compensation was 52.8% of US nonfarm-business output in Q2 2026, the lowest in this BLS series, which begins in 1947.
sources.why: An established direct measure of the income split, with a long baseline before generative AI.
sources.limit: One sector aggregate, not typical pay or AI's effect. The rest of output is not all profit. FRED also publishes an index, which is not a percentage share.
metrics: Nonfarm-business output paid as labour compensation
checks: Confirm the 52.8% level, quarter, sector and series start in BLS Chart Data.
Check numerator/denominator and distinguish percent of output from the FRED index.

sources.title: The world of work and the 2030 Agenda: a ten-year review
sources.locate: March 19, 2026 ILOSTAT review, Labour's share of the economy is shrinking. Both endpoints come from this release.
sources.label: Global labour income share
sources.finding: Global labour income share was 53.0% in 2015 and 52.6% in 2025: down 0.4 percentage points. The ILO describes partial recovery after a sharp decline in 2023.
sources.why: Adds international coverage and estimated self-employed labour income, counterbalancing a US-only story.
sources.limit: Modelled estimates, subject to revision. Two endpoints, not an annual trajectory. Do not splice report vintages or compare the GDP-wide level directly with the BLS sector measure. No AI attribution.
checks: Check both endpoints in the March 2026 release; do not substitute the older 2014-2024 vintage.
Confirm definition and modelled-estimate status; obtain annual data before replacing the two-endpoint chart with a line.

skills.h1: What can people still do when AI is removed?
skills.summary: In one classroom trial, unrestricted GPT reduced later unaided exam scores by 5.4 points out of 100; a guided tutor showed no detectable difference. Long-term skills remain under-measured.
skills.selection: A classroom trial tests learning without AI; a meta-analysis tests when human judgement adds to AI performance. Neither measures long-term skill loss across society.
skills.gap: Follow the same people over time, testing unaided ability as well as AI-assisted performance.

sources.label: Learning without AI
sources.title: Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: Evidence from high school mathematics
sources.finding: The adjusted unaided exam difference was -5.4 points out of 100 for unrestricted GPT, about 17% relative to the no-AI mean. The guided tutor estimate was -0.4 points, not statistically significant.
sources.why: Random assignment and an AI-free exam distinguish help with a task from learning that lasts beyond it.
sources.limit: One school setting and short follow-up; not evidence of permanent or population-wide deskilling. The 17% is relative, not percentage points.
sources.locate: Table 1 column 2: coefficients -0.054/-0.004, SEs 0.022/0.013, control mean 0.321. Multiply by 100 for score points; chart intervals are calculated as estimate +/- 1.96 SE.
checks: Confirm the 17% relative difference and the no-AI comparison group.
Keep the tutor result and short follow-up alongside the harm finding.
metrics: Unaided exam score: unrestricted GPT vs no AI

sources.label: Human-AI judgement
sources.citation: Vaccaro, Almaatouq & Malone (2024), Nature Human Behaviour
sources.title: When combinations of humans and AI are useful: A systematic review and meta-analysis
sources.finding: Human-AI teams outperformed humans alone on average, but underperformed the better of humans or AI alone. Results varied substantially by task.
sources.why: Synthesizes many experiments and separates two easily confused comparison groups.
sources.limit: Task performance, not change in a person's skills over time. Much of the evidence predates current generative AI.
checks: Confirm 106 experiments and the two different baselines.
Check that the page does not describe poorer teamwork as long-term deskilling.
metrics: Standardized effect vs the better of human or AI alone

culture.h1: How much attention goes to AI-made content?
culture.summary: Deezer reports fully AI-generated music at 1–3% of recorded streams, despite over 50% of uploads on peak days. Fraud and platform policy complicate what this says about human attention.
culture.selection: Pair a recurring platform measure of supply and listening with an independent experiment on creative diversity. No single source covers culture as a whole.
culture.gap: Measure what people actually read, watch and hear, and whether human creators retain income and influence.

sources.label: AI music: uploads and listening
sources.title: Deezer will let you fully exclude AI-generated music from your streaming experience
sources.finding: Deezer reports fully AI-generated tracks exceed 50% of uploads on peak days, but account for 1-3% of streams.
sources.why: Separates how much AI content is supplied from how much is played, using a recurring platform disclosure.
sources.limit: One platform and its own detector. Streams may include fraudulent activity; adjustment is unspecified. Recommendation policy also affects listening. Peak-day uploads are not an average.
sources.locate: Notes to editors; FAQ date note
checks: Keep 'on peak days', the August 2026 data date, and the 1-3% stream denominator.
Confirm the fraud and recommendation-policy caveats; do not generalize to all music.

sources.label: Creative diversity
sources.title: Generative AI enhances individual creativity but reduces the collective diversity of novel content
sources.finding: AI-assisted stories received higher creativity ratings, but were more similar to one another than stories written without AI.
sources.why: An independent, preregistered experiment directly tests a possible cultural mechanism, rather than counting AI content alone.
sources.limit: 293 writers producing short stories in one experiment. It does not establish declining diversity across culture or over time.
sources.locate: Results; Figures 2 and 4; Materials and Methods
checks: Confirm the 293 writers and distinction between reader ratings and text similarity.
Keep the creativity benefit as well as the reduced-diversity finding.

institutions.h1: Who makes the decisions when governments use AI?
institutions.summary: The US inventory records 3,611 AI use cases, but not decision volumes or meaningful human control. Its CSV explicitly marks 1,480 deployed or piloted; 338 stages are blank.
institutions.selection: Pair an official disclosure inventory with one concrete operational case. Both are inspectable, but neither is an independent audit of all safeguards.
institutions.gap: Publish decision volumes, human reviews, overrides and appeal outcomes for specific high-impact systems.

sources.title: 2025 Federal Agency AI Use Case Inventory
sources.locate: 2025 inventory README, Summary and agency-table TOTALS; dictionary development_stage, is_high_impact and hi_appeal_process.
sources.label: US federal AI inventory
sources.citation: US Office of Management and Budget (2025 inventory)
sources.date: 2025 inventory; CSV pinned to 14 May 2026 commit
sources.finding: The CSV contains 3,611 rows: 1,040 deployed, 440 pilot, 1,479 pre-deployment, 314 retired and 338 blank stages. The README's 1,818 deployed/piloted total includes the blank-stage cases and cannot be reproduced from explicit stage labels.
sources.why: A reproducible official baseline with public metadata and stage definitions.
sources.limit: Reported uses, not decisions or audited safeguards. Reporting rules change; missing answers do not necessarily mean missing protections.
metrics: Individual reported use cases, all stages
Explicitly deployed or in pilot; 338 stages missing
checks: Reconcile README's 1,818 with 1,480 explicit deployed/pilot CSV rows plus 338 blank stages; inspect data-sourcing notes.
Check stage and safeguard-field definitions; do not count blank fields as failed safeguards.

sources.title: Live Facial Recognition Annual Report September 2025
sources.locate: Annual Report September 2025: PDF page 5, Summary of Results; PDF pages 15-16, False alerts data.
sources.label: AI alerts and human action
sources.finding: London police reported 2,077 facial-recognition alerts, including 10 false alerts. Officers review alerts before deciding whether to approach someone.
sources.why: A concrete case of reported outcomes after AI use, including human checks rather than adoption alone.
sources.limit: One force reporting on its own system. Not a complete override rate, false-negative measure or independent assessment of bias. Arrests are not convictions.
checks: Read PDF page 5 for the period and totals; keep alerts separate from arrests.
Read false-alert details on pages 15-16; do not infer a full override or false-negative rate.

influence.h1: Do people still have a meaningful say?
influence.summary: 57% of US adults reported little or no control over AI's use in their lives in June 2025. This is felt control, not a validated measure of actual decision power.
influence.selection: Use a representative public survey for felt control and a clearly labelled exploratory study for behaviour in conversations. These are proxies, not a validated overall measure.
influence.gap: Connect people's reported control to real choices: the ability to refuse, appeal, reverse a decision or act without AI.

sources.label: Felt control over AI
sources.title: AI in Americans' lives: Awareness, experiences and attitudes
sources.finding: 57% of US adults said they had little or no control over whether AI was used in their lives; 61% wanted more control.
sources.why: A probability-based survey with published questions and methodology, closely related to people's experience of agency.
sources.limit: Perceived control, not observed decision power. One country; this snapshot does not establish a decline caused by AI.
sources.locate: Section on control over AI; linked topline and methodology
checks: Match 57% and 61% to their separate questions and June 2025 fieldwork.
Keep 'felt control' distinct from actual power or proven harm.

sources.label: Disempowerment potential in conversations
sources.title: Who's in Charge? Disempowerment Patterns in Real-World LLM Usage
sources.finding: Automated analysis flagged a small minority of conversations as having severe disempowerment potential, across beliefs, values or actions.
sources.why: Directly operationalizes a form of disempowerment instead of treating AI use alone as evidence of lost agency.
sources.limit: Company classifiers on one service; potential risk is not confirmed harm or lasting loss of influence. Independent replication is needed.
sources.locate: Measuring disempowerment; Prevalence and patterns; paper methods
checks: Check the classifier validation and the distinction between potential and actual harm.
Confirm that conversation rates are not presented as rates of affected people.
